planting.note: Divide 6-inch rhizome sections in spring and plant into a sunken, bottomless-free submerged pot or tub rather than directly into pond mud, since it spreads aggressively and will colonize an entire shoreline.

directions: This architectural, jointed, hollow-stemmed horsetail grows rooted in up to three feet of standing water, giving pond margins and bog gardens a striking vertical, see-through accent where few other plants thrive underwater. Always confine it in a submerged container rather than planting directly into pond mud, since its rhizomes spread aggressively and will colonize an entire shoreline within a few seasons. Cut back old stems in late winter before new growth emerges to keep stands tidy.

planting.note: Divide rhizomes in spring and confine to a sunken container at the pond edge; site away from livestock or horse pasture, since this species is toxic to grazing animals.

directions: A finer-textured, more shade-tolerant horsetail than most of its relatives, this species performs in both full sun and light woodland shade, making it useful for a partly shaded corner of a bog garden. It contains alkaloids and a thiaminase enzyme toxic to livestock and horses, so it should never be planted where grazing animals have access — a genuine safety concern distinct from the usual spread-containment warning for this genus. Like its relatives it spreads by creeping rhizome and is best confined to a sunken container at the pond edge.

planting.note: Direct sow onto exposed mud or in shallow water in spring without burying the seed, which needs light and consistent moisture to germinate.

directions: A native pond-margin perennial with plantain-like leaves and airy panicles of small white flowers, this species offers a North American alternative to the Eurasian water-plantain already common in cultivation. It self-seeds modestly rather than running by rhizome, making it a straightforward, lower-maintenance choice for a native pond edge. Its range from Massachusetts to Minnesota and Florida to Texas means it adapts well to a wide range of regional wetland gardens.

planting.note: Direct sow or divide offsets in spring at the saturated edge of a pond or rain garden where it can sit in shallow water or consistently wet mud.

directions: A larger-flowered, more northerly-adapted cousin of American water-plantain, this species suits colder-climate bog and pond plantings where a bold-leaved marginal perennial is needed. Plant in full sun at the saturated edge of a pond or rain garden; it does not tolerate drying out. It is clump-forming rather than rhizomatous-running, so it poses no containment concerns, unlike several of the more aggressive wetland genera.

planting.note: Divide rhizome sections for the most reliable establishment; seed can be sown 1/4 to 1 inch deep in fall but often needs two winters of cold-moist stratification to germinate.

directions: A grass-like emergent and floating-leaved aquatic distinguished from other bur-reeds already in cultivation by its keeled, unbranched flower spikes, this species softens pond edges while providing fish and invertebrate habitat. Site it at the saturated margin of a pond in full sun to light shade; it adapts between an emergent form in shallow water and a floating-leaved form in deeper water. It spreads only slowly by rhizome compared to cattails or horsetail, posing low containment risk in a bordered pond.

planting.note: Plant tubers 2-4 inches deep directly in pond-edge mud in spring for fastest establishment; seed-grown plants can take two winters to germinate reliably.

directions: A native eastern-US arrowhead with a distinctive five-winged petiole and arrow-shaped leaves, this species gives full sun to light shade at the shallow margin of a pond, tolerating brief inundation but preferring muddy, non-flooded soil most of the season. Its starchy tubers are relished by waterfowl, so expect some predation if ducks visit the pond. Plant tubers directly in spring rather than relying on seed, which germinates slowly and erratically.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Plant peanut-sized tubers in spring at a pond-edge or rain-garden zone that dries to exposed mud between rain events or drawdowns.

directions: Carrying flowers conspicuously blotched yellow-green at the base, this arrowhead is specifically adapted to seasonally exposed mud flats rather than permanently flooded ground, filling a useful niche distinction from always-wet marginal plants. Leaf shape varies with water depth, so expect more arrow-shaped leaves in drier years and more strap-like submersed leaves if briefly flooded. Its tubers are a wildlife food source for waterfowl, like other Sagittaria species.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Divide clumps in spring and plant into consistently wet, muddy soil in full sun; reserve for large wetland restorations or bioswales rather than small residential beds unless contained, since it spreads aggressively by rhizome.

directions: One of the largest native wetland sedges, this species carries a dense fibrous rhizome mat valuable for erosion control and shoreline stabilization, along with attractive arching blue-green foliage. It is a cool-season grower, most active in spring and fall, and serves as a larval host for the Broad-Winged Skipper, Eyed-Brown, and Appalachian Brown butterflies. Because it spreads aggressively by rhizome, reserve it for large wetland restorations, retention ponds, or bioswales rather than small residential beds unless contained.
